t: #3584 Maximum Product of First and Last Elements of a Subsequence — Ordered Suffix Extremes
o: Pick indices i ≤ j with j − i ≥ m − 1 (for m = 1, i = j is allowed) to maximize nums[i]·nums[j]. The separation constraint kills the naive 'two global extremes' idea: in Example 2 the two largest values 5 and 6 are too close together, so the answer uses −5 and −4. The fix is directional: for each legal first index i, the last index lies in the suffix starting at i + m − 1, and depending on the sign of nums[i] we want either the suffix maximum (nums[i] ≥ 0) or suffix minimum (nums[i] < 0). Precomputing suffix max/min makes each evaluation O(1).
k: Legal pairs satisfy j ≥ i + m − 1, so pair each prefix position with a suffix window.
Sign of nums[i] decides whether the suffix max or suffix min is the best partner.
Suffix max/min arrays give O(1) per candidate; m = 1 degenerates to pairing each element with itself.

a.i: Scan from the right building suffix maximum and minimum. For every i in [0, n−m], multiply nums[i] by the extreme of the suffix beginning at i+m−1 chosen by sign. The maximum over all i is the answer.
s: Build smax/smin where smax[i] = max(nums[i:]), smin[i] = min(nums[i:]).
For each i from 0 to n−m, let j = i+m−1.
Candidate = nums[i]·smax[j] if nums[i] ≥ 0 else nums[i]·smin[j].

c.python:
class Solution:
    def maximumProduct(self, nums, m):
        n = len(nums)
        smax = [0] * n
        smin = [0] * n
        smax[n-1] = smin[n-1] = nums[n-1]
        for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):
            smax[i] = max(smax[i+1], nums[i])
            smin[i] = min(smin[i+1], nums[i])
        ans = float('-inf')
        for i in range(n - m + 1):
            j = i + m - 1
            ans = max(ans, nums[i] * smax[j] if nums[i] >= 0 else nums[i] * smin[j])
        return ans

a.t: O(n) — two linear scans (suffix build + evaluation)
a.sp: O(n) for the two suffix arrays

a.n: Approach 2: Running prefix extremes while scanning the last element
a.i: Symmetric formulation: iterate the last index j and maintain the max/min over the eligible prefix nums[0..j−m+1]. Before evaluating j, absorb index j−m+1 into the running extremes, then try both products nums[j]·pmax and nums[j]·pmn — trying both removes the need for sign logic.
s: For j from m−1 to n−1: first fold nums[j−m+1] into pmax/pmn.
Update the answer with nums[j]·pmax and nums[j]·pmn.
a.t: O(n) — single pass with O(1) updates

w: Lead with the suffix-extremes approach; it makes the separation constraint explicit. Common pitfalls: ignoring the j − i ≥ m − 1 gap (the global-two-extremes bug that fails Example 2), mishandling m = 1 (same index twice), and 32-bit overflow since products reach 10^10 — use 64-bit types. Follow-up: return the actual indices, or generalize to k alternating picked elements.
